analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary cutoff below which salaried workers must get overtime pay, and updates it yearly.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in the Education and Workforce Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Salaried workers who earn above a set salary can be denied overtime pay even when they work long hours. The bill would raise that salary cutoff from $35,568 to $45,000 immediately, then step it up to $55,000, $65,000, and $75,000 by 2026, and after 2027 tie it to the 35th-to-55th earnings percentile so it rises automatically with wages [S2][S3]. It would also tighten the duties test so workers who spend 20% or more of their time on ordinary non-managerial work could not be classified as exempt [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning between roughly $35,568 and $75,000 who routinely work more than 40 hours a week would become newly entitled to overtime pay — one-and-a-half times their hourly rate — or to fewer forced overtime hours. The bill's findings note that in 1975, 63% of full-time salaried workers were guaranteed overtime, but by 2022 fewer than 15% were [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the overtime salary threshold from $35,568 to $45,000 on the effective date, then to $55,000 in 2024, $65,000 in 2025, and $75,000 in 2026 [S2][S3].
After 2027, automatically updates the threshold each year to the 55th percentile of weekly earnings for full-time salaried workers, so it no longer erodes between political appointments [S2][S3].

Tightens the duties test: the executive/administrative exemption would not apply if at least 20% of an employee's duties are not directly or closely related to executive or administrative activities [S2][S3].
The bill's findings cite the erosion of overtime coverage: 63% of full-time salaried workers were guaranteed overtime in 1975 versus less than 15% in 2022 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of salaried workers earning below the new thresholds — especially retail, restaurant, hospitality, and other businesses that rely on long-hours salaried managers and staff — would either pay time-and-a-half for overtime hours or cap hours. Workers just above the new thresholds could see their hours trimmed or duties restructured as employers adjust.

drawbacks.text: Employers facing higher overtime costs may respond by cutting salaried workers' hours, converting them to hourly pay with less schedule flexibility, or reclassifying job duties — changes some workers would experience as a loss of flexibility even as pay protection improves [S3].
The threshold jumps from $35,568 to $45,000 within months of enactment, a fast adjustment for employers in lower-wage regions, though the phase-in through 2026 moderates the later steps [S3].

Tying the threshold to the 55th percentile of national earnings means the cutoff could exceed typical salaries in lower-cost states and regions, since the bill uses a national figure and requires only quarterly regional data publication, not regional thresholds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and substantial: millions of salaried workers would gain a legal right to time-and-a-half pay or shorter mandatory hours. The costs are real but conventional — businesses absorb higher labor costs or adjust schedules, which is the normal trade-off of any wage floor. The automatic annual update is a genuine design improvement over past rules, which were rewritten rarely and fell far behind wages. The main honest objection is the speed of the initial jump and the use of a national rather than regional benchmark.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano, joined by Rep. Alma Adams, introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S3][S5].
Twenty-nine House members — all Democrats — cosponsored the bill [S4].
The complete action history shows only introduction and committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of lower-paid salaried workers are better off: the overtime salary threshold stayed at $35,568, so long-hours salaried workers earning above it remain unpaid for overtime, exactly as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who rely on unpaid salaried overtime

for.name: Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: Alma Adams
for.what_they_did: Joined the sponsor in introducing the bill on day one.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee she chaired never held a hearing or markup on the bill and never reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican-run committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: These industries rely heavily on salaried managers and supervisors earning in the $35,000-$75,000 range who routinely work long hours without overtime. The bill would force them to pay time-and-a-half or cap hours, so their interest runs directly against the workers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Low-wage salaried service and office employers generally
industries.note: Any employer using the white-collar exemption to avoid overtime for staff under the new thresholds would face higher payroll costs or scheduling changes. Workers earning above the new cutoffs would not be covered.
